name: Maya Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride a motorbike for two apps, mostly takeaway in the evenings and pharmacy prescriptions in the afternoons, around the inner suburbs. The pharmacy runs are my favourite because the old people are glad to see you and some of them want a chat. I've been doing it eight months, after five years as a barista, and I still mess up the odd address in the big blocks by the station. The worst part is the evening rush when three orders come at once and the app counts every minute.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good, actually. I was careful as a barista and I've got about seven months of costs saved, plus a separate pot for a flat deposit. My partner Leon is a bus mechanic at the depot on Queen's Road, steady job. We're hoping to buy somewhere small in the next two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the usual: I told you so, half the hype was just companies selling stuff. Then I'd talk about something else. I'm not into arguing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay on track. I keep riding, we keep saving, and we buy the flat in two years like we planned. That's a nice feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the pharmacy afternoons and the evening takeaway. Leon and I would keep putting four hundred a month into the deposit pot. I'd maybe do my car licence this year so I'm not stuck on the bike forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, really, because we've worked hard for that flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest pressure on you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices worry me more than AI, because every month the flats we look at go up a bit. And riding in winter, which is cold and a bit dangerous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I use a translation app when customers don't speak English, and I asked a chatbot once why my bike was making a ticking noise. It was right, it was the chain. I wouldn't use it for much more.

say: I'd say half the hype was **companies selling stuff**.
I'd then **change the subject**, because I don't like arguing about it.
think: Things **stay on track**, and we buy the flat in two years.
**House prices** worry me more than AI does.
do: Keep the **pharmacy afternoons** and evening takeaway.
Put **four hundred a month** into the flat deposit pot with Leon.
Take her **car driving test** this year.

The **pharmacy runs** give her real satisfaction.

steps.text: Keep pharmacy deliveries in the afternoon and takeaway at night
Put four hundred a month into the shared flat deposit pot
Buy a small flat with Leon within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change for office people and a smaller one for us, at least for now. I'd tell my old barista friends to watch out for the order screens. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm alright for a while, but I wouldn't want to be riding in five years anyway. The planning side of delivery is already the app's job. It makes me think I should get my car licence sooner and look at other driving work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the car licence this spring and look at patient transport driving, taking people to hospital appointments. I'd ask a woman I know who does it how she got in. Leon and I would still save for the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Things are moving and I want to be one step ahead, not behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is any of your day the thinking kind of work the card mentions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The app picks the order, I ride and hand it over. Maybe the chat with old people at the pharmacy is a sort of thinking work, but no machine is doing that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change the flat plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe we'd buy a bit smaller, to be safe. Leon's job fixing buses feels safe for now.

I'd warn old barista friends about the **order screens**.
think: I'm **alright for a while**, but I don't want to ride in five years.

feel: **Uneasy**, wanting to be one step ahead, not behind.

The **flat purchase** stays central but gets more cautious.

steps.text: Pass the car driving test this spring

Keep four hundred a month going into the deposit pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a sensible plan from the government and companies, not panic. I'd tell people to keep their savings and not do anything stupid. Online I'd mostly read, not post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think riding is finished for me by 2031, and maybe the patient transport driving too a few years later. And Leon fixes buses, but if robots fix buses by then, that's both of us. That's what worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on buying and keep renting. A mortgage on two shaky jobs is a bad idea, so the flat would have to wait. I'd do the car licence and get into patient transport fast, because helping someone off a bus into a clinic seems harder to automate. I'd use a chatbot to help with the application forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a plan I worked hard on suddenly doesn't fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots around 2031. What happens to the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put it on hold. It hurts, because we've saved for three years. But having the deposit money in the bank feels safer than in bricks right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in your life would this hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leon, mostly. And my mum, who works in a supermarket and can't do anything new. I'd worry about her more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get it right, so let's use it. I'd tell friends to learn something new while they still have income. Same as always, nothing too loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's manageable. I could ride two more years, then drive patient transport for a few years. By 2034 I'd want something with people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding, do the car licence this year and start patient transport in a year or two. We'd buy a smaller flat, with a mortgage we could pay on one wage. I'd keep the emergency savings separate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's like a long road you can see the end of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. Does the flat come back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but smaller. One bedroom instead of two, so that one of us could pay the mortgage alone. That's the compromise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to ask her manager about other jobs in the store now, not later. She's fifty-four, and she'd need more time than me. I'd help her with the forms.

say: I'd say there's **time** to get it **right**.
I'd tell friends to **learn something new** while they still earn.
think: It's **manageable**: two more years riding, then patient transport.
By 2034 I'd want **work with people** in it.
do: Buy a **one-bedroom flat** with a mortgage one wage can cover.
feel: **Uneasy** but okay, like a long road with the end in sight.

fieldNote: Five years lets her **keep the flat** plan, scaled down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a reasonable amount of time and we should plan sensibly. I'd tell friends not to panic and not to ignore it. That's me, very middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-nine, and I think I'd be in a different job by then anyway. Ten years feels fine for me and Leon. I'd still want the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the flat in two years as planned. Do the car licence, ride for a few more years, then move into patient transport or ambulance support. Keep saving every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little thoughtful, like when you sign up for something long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years to the robots arriving in 2039. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Leon says people always think they've got more time. I'd want to check every year if things are speeding up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in feeling calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving people to hospital, maybe, or something in the clinic. I want a job where people are glad you came, and the pharmacy runs taught me that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits me and Leon at the same time, just as we're trying to buy a home. What would help is a quick, cheap way to get licences and care qualifications, and banks that don't freeze out young couples with app jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about housing. For people my age, AI is one worry, but getting a home is the big one. The two together are what scares me.

headlineQuote: For people my age, AI is one worry, but getting a home is the big one.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old** motorbike rider doing pharmacy runs and takeaway in the inner suburbs.
She has **seven months saved** plus a flat deposit pot with Leon, a bus mechanic.
She's **steady**, uses AI now and then and leans towards patient transport work.
Her views are **middle-ground**: plan sensibly, don't panic, don't ignore it.
She's calm in slow pictures and **anxious** when both her and Leon's jobs look shaky.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits both of their jobs while they're trying to buy a home.
whatWouldHelp: Banks that don't **freeze out** young couples with app jobs.
